opening.prompt: Scale a mixture or drawing.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make ratios and equivalent ratios necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for ratios and equivalent ratios.
exposition: Compare quantities multiplicatively and preserve the order and meaning of the comparison. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In ratios and equivalent ratios, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Ratio tape diagrams. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Equivalent-ratio table. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Percent as a multiplier
lesson.outcome: Treat percent change as multiplication and distinguish one-time from repeated change.

opening.prompt: Apply tax, discount, markup, and successive changes.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make percent as a multiplier necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for percent as a multiplier.
exposition: Treat percent change as multiplication and distinguish one-time from repeated change. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In percent as a multiplier, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Percent multiplier machine. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Before-after bars. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unit.title: Ratios, Rates, and Linear Relationships

unit.governingQuestion: How do two quantities change together at a constant rate?

lesson.title: Intercepts
lesson.outcome: Find and interpret where one quantity is zero.

opening.prompt: Interpret starting cost, break-even, or depletion points.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make intercepts necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for intercepts.
exposition: Find and interpret where one quantity is zero. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In intercepts, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Context-labeled axis crossings. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Intercept calculation. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Linear models, fit, and residuals
lesson.outcome: Distinguish exact linear relationships from approximate trends and critique extrapolation.

opening.prompt: Fit a line to scattered observations.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make linear models, fit, and residuals necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for linear models, fit, and residuals.
exposition: Distinguish exact linear relationships from approximate trends and critique extrapolation. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In linear models, fit, and residuals, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Scatterplot with fitted line. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Residual arrows. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unit.title: Systems and Simultaneous Constraints
unit.act: Act V - Satisfying several conditions at once
unit.role: Extend linear reasoning to multiple equations, variables, and feasible regions.
unit.governingQuestion: Which values satisfy several requirements simultaneously?
unit.storyArc: Intersections represent simultaneous truth. Graphing estimates solutions, substitution replaces equals by equals, elimination combines equations to remove a variable, and applications reveal when two variables are the natural model.
outcomes: Interpret a system solution as satisfying every constraint.
Solve systems graphically, by substitution, and by elimination.
Classify one, zero, or infinitely many solutions.
Model totals, mixtures, rates, and break-even situations.
Graph systems of inequalities and interpret feasible regions.

unitLessons.title: Systems as simultaneous conditions
unitLessons.outcome: Understand a solution as an ordered pair satisfying every equation or constraint.

opening.prompt: Test a candidate plan against two requirements.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make systems as simultaneous conditions necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for systems as simultaneous conditions.
exposition: Understand a solution as an ordered pair satisfying every equation or constraint. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In systems as simultaneous conditions, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Overlapping constraint cards. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Ordered pair tested in both equations. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

examples.interpretation: The ordered pair is the single point that satisfies both conditions.

unitLessons.title: Substitution
unitLessons.outcome: Replace one variable expression with an equal expression to reduce a system.

opening.prompt: Use one pricing rule inside another total equation.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make substitution necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for substitution.
exposition: Replace one variable expression with an equal expression to reduce a system. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In substitution, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Equation-slot replacement. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Substitution chain. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Substitution
lesson.outcome: Replace one variable expression with an equal expression to reduce a system.

opening.prompt: Use one pricing rule inside another total equation.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make substitution necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for substitution.
exposition: Replace one variable expression with an equal expression to reduce a system. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In substitution, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Equation-slot replacement. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Substitution chain. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Systems strategy studio

opening.prompt: Sort mixed systems and compare methods.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make systems strategy studio necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for systems strategy studio.
exposition: Choose graphing, substitution, or elimination based on structure and purpose. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In systems strategy studio, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Method-selection matrix. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Three-variable extension schematic. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

examples.prompt: A recipe uses 3 cups of water for 5 cups of flour. Find the water needed for 20 cups of flour.
steps: Write the ordered ratio 3/5 = w/20.

examples.answer: 12 cups of water
examples.interpretation: The scale factor from 5 to 20 is 4, so the water quantity also scales by 4.

unitLessons.title: Exponents as repeated multiplication
unitLessons.outcome: Distinguish base, exponent, factors, and value.

opening.prompt: Build area and volume from repeated side lengths.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make exponents as repeated multiplication necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for exponents as repeated multiplication.
exposition: Distinguish base, exponent, factors, and value. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In exponents as repeated multiplication, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Repeated-factor chain. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Square/cube geometry. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

definitions.definition: Distinguish base, exponent, factors, and value. The term names the lesson’s central relationship and the conditions under which its methods are valid.
definitions.conditions: Preserve the original domain, units, grouping, direction, and equivalence conditions whenever they apply.

definitions.definition: A justified change of form that preserves the value, truth set, relationship, or solution information required by the original problem.
definitions.conditions: One-way operations can create candidates and therefore require checking in the original statement.

examples.prompt: Factor x² − 5x + 6 completely and verify the result.
steps: Find two integers whose product is 6 and whose sum is −5.
Write the product (x − 2)(x − 3).
Expand to recover x² − 5x + 6.
examples.interpretation: The factors expose the zeros 2 and 3 while expansion confirms equivalence.

examples.prompt: Represent the result of this exponents as repeated multiplication case in a second form: Factor x² − 5x + 6 completely and verify the result.
steps: Complete the calculation or classification before changing representations.
Choose a table, graph, number line, diagram, or equivalent symbolic form that preserves the same quantities.
Label the input, output, units, restrictions, or endpoints that carry mathematical meaning.
examples.answer: A correctly labeled second representation that preserves (x − 2)(x − 3).
examples.interpretation: The second form must communicate the same relationship, not merely repeat the symbols from the first form.

examples.prompt: A classmate reaches “(x − 2)(x − 3)” in a exponents, roots, and power structure problem. Decide whether the reasoning is valid and justify the decision from the original conditions.
steps: Restate the original condition and identify any domain, unit, sign, or equivalence requirement.
Reproduce the decisive operation using the worked case.
Check the proposed result against the original statement and explain the conclusion.

opening.prompt: Recover side length from area and edge length from volume.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make square roots and nth roots necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for square roots and nth roots.
exposition: Treat roots as inverse questions with principal-root conventions. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In square roots and nth roots, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Square side from area. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Cube side from volume. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

examples.prompt: Simplify 2³ · 2² and explain the exponent law used.
steps: Recognize five repeated factors of 2.
Add the exponents because the bases match.
Evaluate 2⁵.
examples.interpretation: Multiplying powers with the same base combines their repeated factors.

examples.prompt: Represent the result of this square roots and nth roots case in a second form: Simplify 2³ · 2² and explain the exponent law used.
steps: Complete the calculation or classification before changing representations.
Choose a table, graph, number line, diagram, or equivalent symbolic form that preserves the same quantities.
Label the input, output, units, restrictions, or endpoints that carry mathematical meaning.
examples.answer: A correctly labeled second representation that preserves 2⁵ = 32.
examples.interpretation: The second form must communicate the same relationship, not merely repeat the symbols from the first form.

examples.prompt: A classmate reaches “2⁵ = 32” in a exponents, roots, and power structure problem. Decide whether the reasoning is valid and justify the decision from the original conditions.
steps: Restate the original condition and identify any domain, unit, sign, or equivalence requirement.
Reproduce the decisive operation using the worked case.

examples.answer: The result is valid only when the reproduced work and original-condition check both support 2⁵ = 32.
examples.interpretation: A transferred method is complete only after its conditions and conclusion are checked in context.

exposition: Track how an outer exponent applies to every factor. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Scientific notation
lesson.outcome: Represent scale with a normalized coefficient and power of ten.

opening.prompt: Compare astronomical and microscopic measurements.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make scientific notation necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for scientific notation.
exposition: Represent scale with a normalized coefficient and power of ten. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In scientific notation, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Place-value slider. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Power-of-ten scale. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

examples.prompt: Factor x² − 5x + 6 completely and verify the result.
steps: Find two integers whose product is 6 and whose sum is −5.
Write the product (x − 2)(x − 3).
Expand to recover x² − 5x + 6.
examples.interpretation: The factors expose the zeros 2 and 3 while expansion confirms equivalence.

examples.answer: A correctly labeled second representation that preserves (x − 2)(x − 3).

opening.prompt: Observe how equal input steps create unequal output changes.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make power-function preview necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for power-function preview.
exposition: Compare tables and graphs of x, x^2, x^3, and sqrt(x). Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In power-function preview, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Linked tables and graphs. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Symmetry comparison. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unit.title: Polynomial Operations and Special Products
unit.act: Act VII - Building expressions from powers
unit.role: Develop the forward multiplication machinery needed for factoring and quadratics.
unit.governingQuestion: How can expressions built from powers be combined systematically?
unit.storyArc: Polynomials are classified and evaluated, then combined through distribution. Product grids and geometry reveal special products. Division completes the reversible arithmetic of polynomials.
outcomes: Classify and evaluate polynomials.
Add, subtract, and multiply polynomials.
Use exponent laws within monomial operations.
Recognize binomial squares and difference-of-squares products.
Perform polynomial division and verify by multiplication.
unit.investigation: Represent the same polynomial product with distribution, a product grid, and an area model.
unit.mastery: Mixed polynomial operations with missing powers, signs, and verification by reverse operations.

opening.prompt: Sort a collection of algebraic expressions by structure.

exposition: Identify degree, leading term, coefficients, and standard form and distinguish polynomials from other expressions. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In polynomial vocabulary and evaluation, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Polynomial anatomy. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Exponent/coefficient sorting. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unitLessons.title: Division by a monomial
unitLessons.outcome: Divide every polynomial term and state restrictions where needed.

opening.prompt: Reverse a distributed multiplication.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make division by a monomial necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for division by a monomial.
exposition: Divide every polynomial term and state restrictions where needed. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In division by a monomial, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Termwise partition. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Multiply-back check. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

exposition: Combine coefficients and like bases using exponent laws. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In multiplying monomials, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Coefficient/base split. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Repeated-factor consolidation. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

opening.prompt: Divide an algebraic area or expression by a known factor.

exposition: Use place-value alignment to write a polynomial as divisor times quotient plus remainder. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In polynomial long division, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Long-division analogy. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Explicit gaps for missing powers. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unit.title: Polynomial Operations and Special Products
unit.act: Act VII - Building expressions from powers
unit.role: Develop the forward multiplication machinery needed for factoring and quadratics.
unit.governingQuestion: How can expressions built from powers be combined systematically?
unit.storyArc: Polynomials are classified and evaluated, then combined through distribution. Product grids and geometry reveal special products. Division completes the reversible arithmetic of polynomials.
outcomes: Classify and evaluate polynomials.
Add, subtract, and multiply polynomials.
Use exponent laws within monomial operations.
Recognize binomial squares and difference-of-squares products.
Perform polynomial division and verify by multiplication.
unit.investigation: Represent the same polynomial product with distribution, a product grid, and an area model.
unit.mastery: Mixed polynomial operations with missing powers, signs, and verification by reverse operations.

unit.title: Factoring and Quadratic Equations
unit.act: Act VIII - Revealing hidden multiplication
unit.role: Use reverse multiplication to expose zeros and develop the full quadratic-solving toolkit.
unit.governingQuestion: How can hidden product structure reveal solutions?
unit.storyArc: Factoring reverses distribution, then the zero-product property turns factors into solutions. Square roots, completing the square, and the quadratic formula provide increasingly general methods, culminating in strategic choice.
outcomes: Factor using GCF, grouping, trinomial, and special-product methods.
Determine whether factoring is complete in the chosen number system.
Solve quadratics by factoring and the square-root method.
Complete the square geometrically and algebraically.
Derive and use the quadratic formula and discriminant.
unit.investigation: Choose the most efficient method for a mixed set of quadratic equations and defend each choice.
unit.mastery: Students must solve, check, and justify method selection across all four major techniques.

unitLessons.title: Factoring as reverse distribution and GCF
unitLessons.outcome: Rewrite sums as products by extracting the greatest shared factor and verify by expansion.

opening.prompt: Recover rectangle side lengths from an expanded area.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make factoring as reverse distribution and gcf necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for factoring as reverse distribution and gcf.
exposition: Rewrite sums as products by extracting the greatest shared factor and verify by expansion. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In factoring as reverse distribution and gcf, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Rectangle-area factoring. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Shared-factor inventory. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

exposition: Use factor pairs whose product and sum match the trinomial. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In factoring x^2+bx+c, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Area rectangle. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Factor-pair table. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unitLessons.title: Completing the square algebraically
unitLessons.outcome: Translate the geometric construction into a general equation-solving method.

opening.prompt: Solve a quadratic that does not factor cleanly.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make completing the square algebraically necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for completing the square algebraically.
exposition: Translate the geometric construction into a general equation-solving method. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In completing the square algebraically, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Geometry-to-symbol transition. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Balanced addition. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: General factoring strategy and irreducibility
lesson.outcome: Choose factoring methods in order and state what coefficient system is allowed.

opening.prompt: Factor a multistage polynomial until no permitted factors remain.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make general factoring strategy and irreducibility necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for general factoring strategy and irreducibility.
exposition: Choose factoring methods in order and state what coefficient system is allowed. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In general factoring strategy and irreducibility, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Factoring decision tree. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Multistage map. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Solving quadratics by factoring
lesson.outcome: Move all terms to one side, factor, and solve each factor equation.

opening.prompt: Find times or dimensions that make a quadratic quantity zero.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make solving quadratics by factoring necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for solving quadratics by factoring.
exposition: Move all terms to one side, factor, and solve each factor equation. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In solving quadratics by factoring, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Equation-to-zero pipeline. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Factors linked to roots. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

opening.prompt: Solve a quadratic that does not factor cleanly.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make completing the square algebraically necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for completing the square algebraically.
exposition: Translate the geometric construction into a general equation-solving method. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In completing the square algebraically, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Geometry-to-symbol transition. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Balanced addition. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unit.title: Factoring and Quadratic Equations
unit.act: Act VIII - Revealing hidden multiplication
unit.role: Use reverse multiplication to expose zeros and develop the full quadratic-solving toolkit.
unit.governingQuestion: How can hidden product structure reveal solutions?
unit.storyArc: Factoring reverses distribution, then the zero-product property turns factors into solutions. Square roots, completing the square, and the quadratic formula provide increasingly general methods, culminating in strategic choice.
outcomes: Factor using GCF, grouping, trinomial, and special-product methods.
Determine whether factoring is complete in the chosen number system.
Solve quadratics by factoring and the square-root method.
Complete the square geometrically and algebraically.
Derive and use the quadratic formula and discriminant.
unit.investigation: Choose the most efficient method for a mixed set of quadratic equations and defend each choice.
unit.mastery: Students must solve, check, and justify method selection across all four major techniques.

unit.title: Quadratic Functions and Models
unit.act: Act IX - One nonlinear object, several useful forms
unit.role: Connect quadratic equations to parabola geometry, modeling, and optimization.
unit.governingQuestion: What does each algebraic form reveal about a parabola?
unit.storyArc: The same quadratic appears in standard, factored, and vertex forms. Students learn to choose a form based on the information needed, then use parabolas for modeling, inequalities, and regression.
outcomes: Identify vertex, axis, intercepts, opening, and extremum.
Interpret standard, factored, and vertex forms.
Convert among forms strategically.
Build and interpret quadratic models.
Solve quadratic inequalities and critique quadratic fits.
unit.investigation: Build and optimize an area, revenue, or projectile model and interpret all mathematically valid roots.
unit.mastery: Students select and convert forms, graph from structure, solve inequalities, and interpret an optimum with units.

unitLessons.title: Quadratic relations and three useful forms
unitLessons.outcome: Understand that standard, factored, and vertex forms expose different features of one function.

opening.prompt: Compare three formulas for the same trajectory.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make quadratic relations and three useful forms necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for quadratic relations and three useful forms.
exposition: Understand that standard, factored, and vertex forms expose different features of one function. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In quadratic relations and three useful forms, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Same parabola with three formulas. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. exposition: Combine zeros, sign intervals, and graph position to find solution regions. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In quadratic inequalities, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Sign chart. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. exposition: Read shifts, scale, and extrema from a(x-h)^2+k. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In vertex form and transformations, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Parent transformation. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Coordinate mapping. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unit.role: Connect quadratic equations to parabola geometry, modeling, and optimization.
unit.governingQuestion: What does each algebraic form reveal about a parabola?
unit.storyArc: The same quadratic appears in standard, factored, and vertex forms. Students learn to choose a form based on the information needed, then use parabolas for modeling, inequalities, and regression.
outcomes: Identify vertex, axis, intercepts, opening, and extremum.
Interpret standard, factored, and vertex forms.
Convert among forms strategically.
Build and interpret quadratic models.
Solve quadratic inequalities and critique quadratic fits.
unit.investigation: Build and optimize an area, revenue, or projectile model and interpret all mathematically valid roots.
unit.mastery: Students select and convert forms, graph from structure, solve inequalities, and interpret an optimum with units.

lesson.title: Quadratic models and extrema
lesson.outcome: Interpret the vertex as a maximum or minimum in context.

opening.prompt: Model projectile height, area, or revenue.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make quadratic models and extrema necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for quadratic models and extrema.
exposition: Interpret the vertex as a maximum or minimum in context. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In quadratic models and extrema, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Projectile path. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Area/revenue curve. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unit.title: Rational Expressions, Equations, and Variation
unit.act: Act X - Tracking where division is allowed
unit.role: Develop algebra with variable denominators, explicit restrictions, and inverse variation.
unit.governingQuestion: What changes when a variable expression appears in a denominator?
unit.storyArc: A denominator creates excluded inputs. Factoring enables cancellation but cannot restore missing domain points. Common denominators permit addition and equation solving; sign analysis introduces rational inequalities and discontinuities.
outcomes: Identify excluded values and preserve original restrictions.
Simplify and perform arithmetic with rational expressions.
Solve rational equations and check candidate solutions.
Simplify complex rational expressions.
Model variation and interpret holes and asymptotes informally.

unitLessons.title: Rational expressions and restrictions
unitLessons.outcome: Determine where a denominator is zero and state the valid input set.

opening.prompt: Identify forbidden settings in a rate or formula.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make rational expressions and restrictions necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for rational expressions and restrictions.
exposition: Determine where a denominator is zero and state the valid input set. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In rational expressions and restrictions, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Denominator-zero detector. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Domain number line. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

examples.prompt: A recipe uses 3 cups of water for 5 cups of flour. Find the water needed for 20 cups of flour.
steps: Write the ordered ratio 3/5 = w/20.
Multiply both sides by 20.
Check that 12/20 reduces to 3/5.
examples.answer: 12 cups of water
examples.interpretation: The scale factor from 5 to 20 is 4, so the water quantity also scales by 4.

examples.answer: A correctly labeled second representation that preserves 12 cups of water.
examples.interpretation: The second form must communicate the same relationship, not merely repeat the symbols from the first form.

exposition: Assemble an LCD using every factor at its greatest required power. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. unitLessons.title: Rational equations
unitLessons.outcome: Clear denominators to produce candidates and verify every candidate in the original equation.

opening.prompt: Solve a rate or proportion equation with variable denominators.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make rational equations necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for rational equations.
exposition: Clear denominators to produce candidates and verify every candidate in the original equation. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In rational equations, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

LCD applied to equation. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Candidate pipeline. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

opening.prompt: Combine two rational scaling relationships.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make multiplication of rational expressions necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for multiplication of rational expressions.
exposition: Factor before multiplying and cancel across products. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In multiplication of rational expressions, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Factor grid. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Before-after cancellation. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Rational equations
lesson.outcome: Clear denominators to produce candidates and verify every candidate in the original equation.

opening.prompt: Solve a rate or proportion equation with variable denominators.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make rational equations necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for rational equations.
exposition: Clear denominators to produce candidates and verify every candidate in the original equation. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In rational equations, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

LCD applied to equation. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Candidate pipeline. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for rational inequalities and introductory graphs.
exposition: Use zeros and restrictions as critical values and distinguish holes from vertical asymptotes. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In rational inequalities and introductory graphs, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Sign chart. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Hole/asymptote comparison. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

unit.title: Rational Expressions, Equations, and Variation
unit.act: Act X - Tracking where division is allowed
unit.role: Develop algebra with variable denominators, explicit restrictions, and inverse variation.
unit.governingQuestion: What changes when a variable expression appears in a denominator?
unit.storyArc: A denominator creates excluded inputs. Factoring enables cancellation but cannot restore missing domain points. Common denominators permit addition and equation solving; sign analysis introduces rational inequalities and discontinuities.
outcomes: Identify excluded values and preserve original restrictions.
Simplify and perform arithmetic with rational expressions.
Solve rational equations and check candidate solutions.
Simplify complex rational expressions.
Model variation and interpret holes and asymptotes informally.
unit.investigation: Compare equivalent-looking rational formulas and explain how a missing input changes the graph or context.
unit.mastery: Every answer must include restrictions and rational-equation candidates must be checked in the original equation.

unit.title: Radicals, Rational Exponents, and Complex Numbers
unit.shortTitle: Radicals, Rational Exponents, and Complex Numbers
unit.act: Act XI - Reversing powers and enlarging the number system
unit.role: Develop exact root arithmetic, radical equations, extraneous-solution logic, and basic complex arithmetic.
unit.governingQuestion: How do we reverse powers, and what happens when the real numbers are insufficient?
unit.storyArc: General roots and rational exponents express inverse powers. Radical arithmetic creates exact forms, conjugates rationalize denominators, and raising powers solves equations but may introduce candidates. Complex numbers complete quadratic solutions.
outcomes: Interpret principal and general roots.
Simplify and combine radical expressions.
Rationalize denominators using factors or conjugates.
Connect radicals and rational exponents.
Solve radical equations and perform basic complex arithmetic.
unit.investigation: Compare reversible and nonreversible algebraic steps and explain exactly where extraneous candidates enter.
unit.mastery: Students preserve domains, simplify exact forms, check radical candidates, and express nonreal quadratic roots correctly.

exposition: Distinguish the principal root operation from finding every solution of a power equation. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. examples.prompt: A recipe uses 3 cups of water for 5 cups of flour. Find the water needed for 20 cups of flour.

exposition: Simplify first and combine only like radical terms. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In adding and subtracting radicals, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. Radical tiles. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Canonical-form matching. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

exposition: Interpret the denominator of an exponent as a root and the numerator as a power. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. unit.act: Act XI - Reversing powers and enlarging the number system
unit.role: Develop exact root arithmetic, radical equations, extraneous-solution logic, and basic complex arithmetic.
unit.governingQuestion: How do we reverse powers, and what happens when the real numbers are insufficient?
unit.storyArc: General roots and rational exponents express inverse powers. Radical arithmetic creates exact forms, conjugates rationalize denominators, and raising powers solves equations but may introduce candidates. Complex numbers complete quadratic solutions.
outcomes: Interpret principal and general roots.
Simplify and combine radical expressions.
Rationalize denominators using factors or conjugates.
Connect radicals and rational exponents.
Solve radical equations and perform basic complex arithmetic.
unit.investigation: Compare reversible and nonreversible algebraic steps and explain exactly where extraneous candidates enter.

opening.prompt: Decompose an area or length under a radical.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.

exposition: Extract perfect-power factors and retain exact form. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In simplifying radicals, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Factor tree under radical. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Square-area decomposition. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

lesson.title: Adding and subtracting radicals
lesson.outcome: Simplify first and combine only like radical terms.

opening.prompt: Combine exact geometric lengths.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make adding and subtracting radicals necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for adding and subtracting radicals.
exposition: Simplify first and combine only like radical terms. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In adding and subtracting radicals, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Radical tiles. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Canonical-form matching. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.
